demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For an index trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is a poor fit unless the death involved clear interpersonal wrongdoing by a trusted person; nothing else in the profile supports that specific circumstance, so this item is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'Need to stay alert' at bedtime implies ongoing external danger, which is less coherent with bereavement-related trauma in the absence of any triggers or appraisals about current interpersonal/physical threat. The rest of the profile centers on loss, self-blame, fragmented reliving memory, and catastrophic interpretations of delay, making this item stand out as mismatched.

vignette:
Amara

Amara's mother collapsed during a routine clinic visit on a Tuesday afternoon in March. Amara was not there. She was in the field that day, conducting soil samples in a wetland restoration site two hours north of the city, her hands in the earth, her mind focused on pH levels and microbial counts. The call came at 3:47 p.m. from a hospital number she didn't recognize. Her mother had suffered a massive stroke. By the time Amara arrived at the hospital, her mother was gone.

In the weeks that followed, Amara found herself replaying the morning before she left for work. Her mother had asked her to stay home that day—nothing specific, just a feeling, she'd said. Amara remembered this now with a weight that felt unbearable. She had been irritable that morning, eager to get to the site, and she had dismissed her mother's request with the kind of casual indifference that adult children sometimes show. If she had stayed. If she had listened. If she had been there, perhaps she would have noticed something—a slur in her mother's speech, a weakness on one side—something that would have changed everything. Amara had come to believe with absolute certainty that her mother's death was a direct consequence of her own carelessness, her own failure to be present. She was the kind of person who prioritized work over family, who couldn't be bothered to listen to her mother's intuition. That kind of person deserved what had happened.

The rumination was relentless. Amara would lie awake at night—when she could sleep at all, which was rarely—constructing elaborate scenarios in which she had made different choices. She picked arguments with her colleagues about nothing, manufactured small dramas around lab protocols and data entry, anything to occupy the space in her mind that would otherwise fill with the thought of her mother alone in that clinic room. She stopped watching television, stopped scrolling through news feeds. Any story about sudden death, about medical emergencies, about families torn apart by circumstance, triggered a response so visceral that her body would move before her mind could catch up—her heart racing, her hands shaking, a sensation of drowning even though she was sitting safely at her desk.

When something took longer than expected—a delayed email response, a slow traffic light, a colleague running late to a meeting—Amara's mind immediately spiraled into catastrophe. Something bad was happening. Someone was hurt. She had learned not to trust the ordinary rhythms of the day.

The memory itself was strange and fragmented. Amara could recall certain details with photographic precision: the way the hospital waiting room smelled, the color of the nurse's scrubs, the exact phrasing of the words "I'm so sorry." But the larger narrative of her mother's death—the sequence of events, the medical explanation, the finality of it—seemed to slip away whenever she tried to grasp it fully. Her mind would push the memory away before she could complete it, as though some part of her could not bear the full weight of what had happened. And when she tried to explain it to anyone—to friends, to her supervisor, to the few people who had asked how she was managing—the words simply would not come. She knew what had happened. She lived inside it every moment. But describing it aloud felt impossible, as though the event existed in a space beyond language.

Most disturbing was the quality of the memory itself. When it surfaced unbidden, it did not feel like something that had happened three months ago. It felt like it was happening now. She was in the hospital again, receiving that news again, her mother was dying again, and there was nothing she could do to stop it. The past and present had collapsed into a single, ongoing moment.

Amara had taken a leave of absence from her position at the environmental consulting firm. She had stopped returning calls from friends. She had convinced herself that someone else—someone more attentive, more worthy, more present—would never have let this happen. The injustice of it consumed her: that her mother had died in a clinic, that no one had been held responsible, that the world had simply moved on. Amara remained stuck, unable to move forward, unable to move backward, her body and mind locked in a state of perpetual emergency. It was only when her sister, frightened by Amara's increasing isolation and the raw desperation in her voice during their last phone call, insisted she speak to someone that Amara finally made an appointment. She didn't know if therapy could change anything. But she was terrified of what would happen if nothing did.
